extracted.intended_audience: legislators, statesmen, and the educated public concerned with the French Revolution and government policy
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th‑century political pamphlet offering prescriptive judgments about constitutional design, civil–military relations, municipal power, and public finance in revolutionary France. The text sets out what good (and bad) governance looks like and warns of political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army must act only as an instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: "The nature of things requires that the army should never act but as an instrument."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The army must be subordinated to civilian authority and used as a tool of the state; if it 'erects itself into a deliberate body' and acts on its own resolutions it will create a 'military democracy' that will devour those who produced it. This is presented as a chief rule of civil–military relations and a test of constitutional health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent soldiers' irregular consultations and 'democratic assemblies' (comices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'irregular consultations and turbulent committees formed in some regiments by the common soldiers and non-commissioned officers'—the 'monstrous democratic assemblies [comitia, comices]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such assemblies undermine discipline, encourage mutiny, and have led to murders of commanders; they are portrayed as symptomatic of a deeper political degeneration and a direct threat to the state. The text treats them as an anti-pattern requiring strong prevention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit municipal authority over troops to requisition only
rubrics_metrics.description: "You have bounded the action which you have permitted to the latter over the former to the right of requisition; but never did the letter or the spirit of your decrees authorize the commons ... to break the officers, to try them, to give orders to the soldiers..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipalities must not assume powers over military command (trying or breaking officers, giving orders, driving soldiers from posts). Granting municipalities control over troops destroys the chain of military subordination and creates conflicting authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use civic clubbing/feasting to restore military discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The king's circulars propose that regiments 'should join themselves with the clubs and confederations ... and mix with them in their feasts and civic entertainments.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing soldiers with municipal festive societies may make them 'admirable citizens' but will not make them 'good soldiers'; rather it weakens obedience to officers and fuses military conspiracies with civic sedition. This policy is criticized as an ineffective and dangerous remedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Officers must be the primary object of soldiers' loyalty (avoid electioneering management)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To secure a real army, the officer should be first and last in the eye of the soldier... They are to manage their troops by electioneering arts. They must bear themselves as candidates, not as commanders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commanders must be perceived as commanders, not elected representatives or candidates; managing troops through electoral/patronage arts will transform officers into factional actors and erode discipline and respect essential for military efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sovereign (king) must have real, vigorous, personal authority over the army
rubrics_metrics.description: "A king is not to be deposed by halves... They must be constrained ... by a real, vigorous, effective, decided, personal authority."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nominal or captive monarch is ineffective as head of the army; absent real personal authority, the army will either despise or install another master (a popular general) who will dominate the state. Personal, decisive authority is presented as necessary to maintain proper military command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dual patronage of officer appointment (king + Assembly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution gives provisional nomination to the king 'with a reserve of approbation by the National Assembly', creating a double negotiation for rank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divided or competing appointment channels (court and Assembly) promote intrigue and faction within the officer corps: those favored by one power will oppose the other, poisoning military cohesion and creating political factionalism inside the army.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make seniority the sole rule for promotion
rubrics_metrics.description: "If ... you will have no other rule for command or promotion than seniority, you will have an army of formality; at the same time it will become more independent and more of a military republic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotion by seniority alone produces formal but politically independent officers and can foster a quasi-republican military spirit; this is an undesirable trade-off and not a remedy for faction or weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transient/popular assemblies cannot reliably command armies
rubrics_metrics.description: Armies 'will least of all yield [obedience] to an Assembly which is to have only a continuance of two years.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-lived, transient, or popular legislative bodies lack the stable authority and permanence needed to command military obedience; this instability encourages the rise of charismatic generals who command by personal authority rather than constitutional legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching soldiers abstract 'rights' without preserving the principle of obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Telling the soldier he is 'a citizen, and has the rights of man and citizen' undermines the 'principle of obedience' by encouraging him to see himself as his own governor and to claim choice over his officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political instruction that emphasizes individual rights without maintaining military subordination will produce soldiers inclined to elect or reject officers, exercise negatives over kings, and align with municipal forces—thus destabilizing military hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on proclamations and oaths alone to secure obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: After reporting the soldiers 'trampled upon the decrees of the Assembly', the Assembly 'renew decrees and proclamations ... they multiply oaths in proportion as they weaken in the minds of men the sanctions of religion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal proclamations and multiplied oaths are ineffective remedies for deep disorder and may even weaken moral sanctions; proper enforcement (courts, martial law where warranted) and substantive measures are necessary rather than rhetorical or ceremonial repetitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using the army primarily for internal coercion while preaching non-violence toward citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly has 'taught ... troops ought not to fire on citizens' yet will 'call out troops to act against his people' (and to coerce colonists, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contradictory doctrines—preaching that troops should not fire on citizens while deploying them for domestic coercion—undermine legitimacy and create cycles of repression and revolt; practical consequences (massacres, tortures) follow when rhetoric and policy conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: The municipal (district) army's democratic constitution is dangerous in relation to national coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The municipal army is 'a mere democratic body, unconnected with the crown or the kingdom' which, in relation to the crown, Assembly, tribunals, or other army, 'seems a monster' and risks national calamity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locally controlled, democratically officered militias uncoordinated with national institutions create competing sovereignties and incoherence between parts of the state; they are presented as a worse preservative of constitution than other bad historical examples (systasis of Crete, confederation of Poland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of a financier: secure, impose, employ revenue; secure credit foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The objects of a financier are, then, to secure an ample revenue; to impose it with judgment and equality; to employ it economically; and when necessity obliges him to make use of credit, to secure its foundations ... by the clearness and candor of his proceedings, the exactness of his calculations, and the solidity of his funds."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public finance is central to state capacity and public virtue. A finance minister's duties are practical and tested by securing sufficient revenue, fair/impartial taxation, economical expenditure, and—when borrowing is necessary—transparent accounting, accurate calculations, and solid funding to preserve credit and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not preach abstract metaphysical rights while withholding redress or making selective property rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders teach people to abhor feudalism and declare rights, yet refrain from abolishing rents and then use troops to enforce new property arrangements; peasants see contradictions and may resist payment of rents or taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistency between universal declarations of rights and selective application (protecting some property while depriving others) breeds resentment and resistance among the populace; coherent policy and provision for redress are necessary to avoid revolt and loss of legitimacy.
